title: Looking back: year two
hook: the Buddha's words, read in order
tomorrow: which beginner sent the Buddha his two chief disciples?

segments.voice: Yesterday, year one: the stories, the first practices, the first verses. The first mountain. Today, the year you read the Buddha's discourses in order.
screen: `THE FIRST MOUNTAIN.` → `YEAR TWO: HIS OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: Four tabs open, four reviews of the same thing, each one sure the others are wrong. A town in the suttas lived with that. Wandering teachers kept passing through Kesaputta, each praising his own teaching and running down the rest. So the Kalamas, the people there, went to the Buddha and said it plainly: we're in doubt. Which of these teachers is speaking the truth? He's one more teacher passing through. They're asking him to judge his rivals. What he says next is not what a salesman would say.
screen: `FOUR TABS, FOUR REVIEWS.` → `EACH TEACHER RUNS DOWN THE REST.` → `"WE'RE IN DOUBT."`

segments.voice: He says: it's fitting that you doubt. Then he lists what not to lean on by itself: what you've heard over and over, tradition, rumor, a scripture, clever reasoning, a view you already like, a speaker who seems capable, even the thought, this monk is our teacher. Instead, he says, when you know for yourselves that a thing is unwholesome, blamed by the wise, and leads to harm when taken up, let it go. When you know it leads to welfare and happiness, take it up. And he doesn't leave them alone with that. He walks them through it. Greed, hatred, delusion: when they arise in a person, is it for welfare or for harm? Harm, they say. And someone free of them? Welfare. They worked it out themselves, with him asking the questions. Notice what he didn't say. He didn't tell them to throw out every teacher, or to trust their gut alone. He pointed to what the wise blame and praise, and asked them to look. That's year two in one scene. The Buddha's own words, read in order, keep handing the test back. Buddhists have a word for the teaching that fits: ehipassiko, come and see. Not take my word for it. Come and see. So reading the suttas isn't the opposite of testing them. It's how the testing starts.
screen: `"IT'S FITTING THAT YOU DOUBT."` · `KNOW FOR YOURSELVES.` · `GREED, HATRED, DELUSION: HARM.` · `EHIPASSIKO: COME AND SEE.` · then, large: `HIS OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: Find a pen and anything to write on. Write one line of the Buddha's that you've actually tried in your own life, and under it, in a few words, what you saw happen. Then rest your eyes on the page for the rest of the sit, the words and the test side by side.
Looking back, at year two: the discourses read in order, and the morning he told the Kalamas to see for themselves.
Your line: his own words. Read them, then let your life do the checking. Two days up the summit.

screen: `DAY 1779 COUNTS.` → `THE SUMMIT · 2 OF 14.` → `TOMORROW: WHICH BEGINNER SENT THE BUDDHA HIS TWO CHIEF DISCIPLES?`

howItsDone: Buddhists read and chant the suttas at home and in temples; some teachers point to the Kalama Sutta when they invite students to test a teaching in their own practice.

match.prompt: the Kalamas' question — tap the pairs.
pairs: each praised his own, ran down the rest

myth: the Kalama Sutta says trust nothing but your own gut
it says know for yourselves what leads to harm or welfare, and it names what the wise blame. then he walks them through it.
the Buddha told the Kalamas their doubt was fitting
his first answer: it's fitting that you doubt.

fork.setup: your cousin swears by a morning routine from a video and wants you to try it because the guy has a huge following. what would the Kalama test ask first?
options: when you actually do it, what does it lead to: harm, or welfare?
how big the following is; that many people can't all be wrong.
nothing; the Buddha said never to try what anyone tells you.
fork.reveal: not the crowd, and not 'trust nothing'. the Buddha told the Kalamas to watch what a thing does when taken up: harm, or welfare.

original.note: Pali: come and see; said of the teaching, which invites you to look for yourself.

trapdoor: what you thought: looking back means remembering what you read.
what it means: year two read the Buddha's words in order, and in the Kalama Sutta he hands the test back: know for yourselves.
what a scholar hears: 'know for yourselves' comes paired with 'blamed or praised by the wise', so the sutta isn't a call to go it alone.
guess: turning to a past year of the path to see what it gave
giving up on the path once a hard stretch has begun
measuring yourself against how others have done

chat.says: sorting old sketchbooks for the senior show. ông reads suttas nightly. didn't the Buddha say don't just believe him?
options: he said test it, not skip it. ông reads the words, then checks them in his life.
right, so reading is pointless. trust your gut and leave the suttas alone.
he said believe it because he's the Buddha; doubting him shows weak faith.
chat.meaning: The Buddha told the Kalamas not to go by scripture alone, but to know for themselves what leads to harm or welfare. Reading starts the test.

tie.story: The Kalamas doubted the teachers; the Buddha called their doubt fitting and walked them through testing greed, hatred and delusion.
tie.friend: Mai can see ông's nightly reading as half the test; the other half is how he lives.
tie.you: which teaching have you actually tested?

Kesaputta.meaning: a town in the Buddha's time, home of the Kalamas

Kalamas.meaning: the people of Kesaputta who asked the Buddha which teacher to trust

ehipassiko.meaning: come and see: the teaching invites you to look for yourself

suttas.meaning: the recorded discourses of the Buddha

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 3.65 (Kalama Sutta, also called Kesaputtiya Sutta)
Majjhima Nikaya 7 (the recollection of the Dhamma: 'come and see')

notes: AN 3.65 paraphrased: the Kalamas say teachers come to Kesaputta each extolling their own doctrine and disparaging others'; the Buddha says doubt is fitting; the list of ten things not to go by (oral tradition, lineage, report, scripture, logic, inference, reasoning by appearances, agreement with a view, a capable-seeming speaker, 'the ascetic is our teacher') is compressed; then the questioning on greed, hatred and delusion. Confirm the compression is fair.
Ehipassiko from the standard recollection of the Dhamma (e.g. MN 7). Confirm.
Trapdoor floor 3: the sutta's criterion pairs 'knowing for yourselves' with 'censured/praised by the wise' (viññugarahita / viññuppasattha). Confirm.

Shape: story (the Kalamas' question told as one scene; the hook ends on the cliffhanger the teach answers). Mai's two-week storyline (days 1779-1791): her last weeks of high school: the senior art show, ông, Ava, leaving home in the fall, graduation. Here she sorts five years of sketchbooks for the show.
Surprising fact: the Buddha's first answer to people doubting every teacher, himself included, was that their doubt was fitting.
